attestations.source_text: The verb être (to be) The verbs être (to be) and avoir (to have) are essential verbs you need to memorize. They are both irregular. Let’s start with être: je suis / I am / nous sommes / we are / tu es / you are (familiar) / vous êtes / you are / il/elle est / he/she is / ils/elles sont / they are

The verb avoir (to have) The verb avoir (to have) also has an irregular conjugation. j’ai / I have / nous avons / we have / tu as / you have / vous avez / you have / il/elle a / he/she has / ils/elles ont / they have
The -oir verbs The -oir verbs do not all follow the same conjugation pattern. We’ll start with the very useful verb savoir (to know).

Savoir means to know a fact, to know how to do something from memory or study. je sais / I know / nous savons / we know / tu sais / you know / vous savez / you know / il/elle sait / he/she knows / ils/elles savent / they know

Connaître means to know, to be acquainted with, to be familiar with. In a figurative way, it means to enjoy, to experience. It is always followed by a direct object; it is never followed by a dependent clause. je connais / I know / nous connaissons / we know / tu connais / you know / vous connaissez / you know / il/elle connaît / he/she knows / ils/elles connaissent / they know
Pouvoir (can, may) expresses ability and capability. je peux / I can / nous pouvons / we can / tu peux / you can / vous pouvez / you can / il/elle peut / he/she can / ils/elles peuvent / they can

A number of other verbs ending in -oir are irregular. Let’s look at a few examples in their first-person singular and plural forms: apercevoir to see, to perceive / j’aperçois / I see, I perceive / nous apercevons / we see, we perceive / décevoir to disappoint / je déçois / I disappoint / nous décevons / we disappoint / devoir must, to have to / je dois / I must, I have to / nous devons / we must, we have to / émouvoir to move, to stir / j’émeus / I move, I stir / nous émouvons / we move, we stir / prévoir to foresee, to predict / je prévois / I foresee / nous prévoyons / we foresee / promouvoir to promote / je promeus / I promote / nous promouvons / we promote / recevoir to receive / je reçois / I receive / nous recevons / we receive / valoir to be worth / cela vaut / it is worth / nous valons / we are worth / voir to see / je vois / I see / nous voyons / we see
Falloir and pleuvoir are used only in the third-person singular. falloir / to be necessary / il faut / it is necessary / pleuvoir / to rain / il pleut / it is raining

concepts.name: Essential French verbs
concepts.description: Verbs that are fundamental and must be memorized: être and avoir.

attestations.source_text: The verbs être (to be) and avoir (to have) are essential verbs you need to memorize.

concepts.name: Present tense
concepts.description: Conjugation of verbs in the present tense, focusing on irregular forms.

attestations.source_text: Let’s start with être: je suis / I am / nous sommes / we are...

concepts.name: Irregular verbs
concepts.description: Verbs that do not follow regular conjugation patterns, especially -oir verbs.

attestations.source_text: The -oir verbs do not all follow the same conjugation pattern.

concepts.name: Negation
concepts.description: Use of ne...pas and the change of partitive articles to de/d' after negation.

attestations.source_text: Note that un, une, and des change to de or d’ when the verb is in the negative form.

concepts.name: Idiomatic expressions with avoir
concepts.description: Common expressions using avoir to describe states, feelings, needs, and age.

attestations.source_text: The verb avoir is used in many common idiomatic expressions. Here are a few examples: j’ai de la chance / I am lucky...

concepts.name: Savoir vs. connaître
concepts.description: Distinction between knowing facts/how to do something (savoir) and being acquainted with (connaître).

attestations.source_text: When learning the verb savoir, you also need to become acquainted with the verb connaître, in order to understand when to use one or the other.

concepts.name: Modal verbs
concepts.description: Verbs expressing ability, permission, desire: pouvoir, vouloir, devoir, savoir.

attestations.source_text: Pouvoir (can, may) expresses ability and capability. The verb vouloir (to want) is used to express wishes and desires.

concepts.name: Impersonal verbs
concepts.description: Verbs used only in the third-person singular: falloir, pleuvoir.

attestations.source_text: Falloir and pleuvoir are used only in the third-person singular.

grammar_rules.summary: Conjugation of être in the present tense.
grammar_rules.explanation: Être is an irregular verb. Its present tense forms are: je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont.
grammar_rules.formation: je suis / tu es / il/elle est / nous sommes / vous êtes / ils/elles sont
usage: To express identity, nationality, profession, state, etc.
common_traps: The -s of vous is pronounced as a z when followed by the vowel ê- in êtes.

attestations.source_text: je suis / I am / nous sommes / we are / tu es / you are (familiar) / vous êtes / you are / il/elle est / he/she is / ils/elles sont / they are

grammar_rules.summary: Conjugation of avoir in the present tense.
grammar_rules.explanation: Avoir is an irregular verb. Its present tense forms are: j'ai, tu as, il/elle a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont.
grammar_rules.formation: j'ai / tu as / il/elle a / nous avons / vous avez / ils/elles ont
usage: To express possession, age, states, idiomatic expressions.
common_traps: The -s of nous, vous, ils, elles is pronounced z when followed by a vowel.

attestations.source_text: j’ai / I have / nous avons / we have / tu as / you have / vous avez / you have / il/elle a / he/she has / ils/elles ont / they have

grammar_rules.summary: After negation, un, une, des change to de or d'.
grammar_rules.explanation: When a verb is negated, the indefinite articles un, une, des become de (or d' before a vowel).
conditions: Applies to direct objects after negated verbs.

attestations.source_text: Note that un, une, and des change to de or d’ when the verb is in the negative form. Tu as des amis à Paris? Non, je n’ai pas d’amis à Paris.

grammar_rules.summary: Expression to indicate pain or trouble doing something.
grammar_rules.explanation: Avoir mal à + body part indicates pain. Avoir du mal à + infinitive indicates difficulty doing something.
grammar_rules.formation: avoir mal à + article + body part; avoir du mal à + infinitive

attestations.source_text: When referring to the state of one’s body, French uses avoir mal à (having an ache or pain). J’ai mal à la tête. Il a mal au bras. When avoir mal à is followed by a verb, it means to have trouble doing something. Nous avons du mal à accepter sa décision. Elle a du mal à monter l’escalier.

grammar_rules.summary: Savoir is used before an infinitive or dependent clause to express knowing how to or knowing a fact.
grammar_rules.explanation: Savoir can be translated as 'can' when followed by an infinitive. It is the only verb that can be used before a dependent clause or an infinitive to mean 'know'.
usage: To express ability to do something
common_traps: Savoir is sometimes translated by can.

attestations.source_text: Note that savoir is sometimes translated by can. Before a dependent clause or before an infinitive, only savoir can be used. Je ne sais pas où il est. Il sait qu’elle est occupée.

grammar_rules.summary: Connaître is always followed by a direct object, never by a dependent clause.
grammar_rules.explanation: Connaître means to know, to be acquainted with, or to be familiar with. It cannot be followed by a clause; it requires a noun or pronoun as direct object.
usage: To express familiarity with people, places, things
restrictions: Never followed by a dependent clause
common_traps: Do not use connaître before an infinitive or clause; use savoir.

attestations.source_text: It is always followed by a direct object; it is never followed by a dependent clause.

grammar_rules.summary: Conjugation of pouvoir in the present tense.
grammar_rules.explanation: Pouvoir expresses ability and capability. Its present forms are: je peux, tu peux, il/elle peut, nous pouvons, vous pouvez, ils/elles peuvent.
grammar_rules.formation: je peux / tu peux / il/elle peut / nous pouvons / vous pouvez / ils/elles peuvent
exceptions: In formal inversion, first-person singular becomes 'puis-je'.
common_traps: Use 'puis-je' instead of 'peux-je' for formal inversion.

attestations.source_text: Pouvoir (can, may) expresses ability and capability. je peux / I can / nous pouvons / we can / tu peux / you can / vous pouvez / you can / il/elle peut / he/she can / ils/elles peuvent / they can

grammar_rules.summary: Conjugation of vouloir in the present tense.
grammar_rules.explanation: Vouloir expresses wishes and desires. Its present forms are: je veux, tu veux, il/elle veut, nous voulons, vous voulez, ils/elles veulent.
grammar_rules.formation: je veux / tu veux / il/elle veut / nous voulons / vous voulez / ils/elles veulent

attestations.source_text: The verb vouloir (to want) is used to express wishes and desires. je veux / I want / nous voulons / we want / tu veux / you want / vous voulez / you want / il/elle veut / he/she wants / ils/elles veulent / they want

exceptions_and_traps.title: Savoir vs. Connaître
exceptions_and_traps.description: Savoir is used for knowing facts or knowing how to do something; it can be followed by an infinitive or clause. Connaître means to be acquainted with and is always followed by a direct object, never a clause.

attestations.source_text: When learning the verb savoir, you also need to become acquainted with the verb connaître, in order to understand when to use one or the other. Connaître means to know, to be acquainted with, to be familiar with. It is always followed by a direct object; it is never followed by a dependent clause.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Article change in negation
exceptions_and_traps.description: After a negated verb, un, une, des become de or d'.

attestations.source_text: Note that un, une, and des change to de or d’ when the verb is in the negative form.

exceptions_and_traps.title: Puis-je for formal inversion
exceptions_and_traps.description: In formal inversion, the first-person singular of pouvoir becomes 'puis-je' instead of 'peux-je'.

attestations.source_text: When asking permission with inversion in formal style, the first-person singular of pouvoir takes a different form. Puis-je vous aider?
